newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori hits road to shed crisis woes.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori hits road to shed crisis woes.

text.p: The pure, dry air of the Andean highlands had probably never felt so good to Peru's troubled President Alberto Fujimori.

His serious countenance, furrowed by four weeks of dealing with his country's hostage crisis, turned to brief smiles of pleasure as he emerged from the presidential helicopter on a recent trip to the remote mountain community of Vilcashuaman.

Within minutes Fujimori was pressing hands, making speeches, donning local costume and dancing with peasant women. "Long live the president! Long live Fujimori!" shouted the ecstatic crowd of Vilcashuaman peasants. "'Chinaman', we love you" cried a boy, using Fujimori's popular nickname.
It was Fujimori's first time outside the capital Lima since the start of the rebel siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence, and clearly a relief.
After briefly -- and uncharacteristically -- lying low in the early stages of the hostage crisis, Fujimori was back on the road in style, doing what he likes best.

First he led a chaotic caravan of journalists and officials round Lima's impoverished shantytowns to demonstrate his popular support and scorn for the rebels holding 74 VIP hostages at the diplomatic residence.
Then he travelled to Vilcashuaman to remind the world of his victory over leftist guerrillas who until recently controlled large swathes of the surrounding highlands.
For Fujimori, who has made his near-daily visits to the provinces and poor outskirts of Lima a hallmark of his six-year presidency, it was back to business as usual.
"The Peruvian people reject violence," he told several thousand Andean peasants packed into the central square of Vilcashuaman after inaugurating an orphanage for victims of the guerrilla conflict.
To the peasants' delight, Fujimori and Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram, who was accompanying him, donned a traditional cloak and hat while clambering up Inca ruins.
"I just can't believe they are here. It's like a dream," said Miguel Jimenez, a peasant farmer in Vilcashuaman pushing through the crowd to try to reach Fujimori.

Fujimori's flamboyant return to the public arena came after weeks of deliberate isolation and silence as he worked out a strategy against the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding the diplomatic residence.
His public appearances were aimed at restoring confidence to Peruvians shocked and depressed by the MRTA assault, and act as a counter-salvo to the rebels' propaganda offensive.
But the resurrection of the Fujimori roadshow was merely a continuation of a well-honed style.

"This has always been his tactic," said political analyst Jorge Aragon. "In this respect, Fujimori tries to distinguish himself from all the presidents before him. He wants to show that he cares about the forgotten, isolated parts of Peru, and about the poor people. He wants his presence to be felt even in the most distant places."
Fujimori first developed the tactic in his 1990 presidential election campaign, using a tractor to attend rallies and address crowds in shantytowns.

His populist style, combined with advances against the guerrillas and economic reforms, helped him to a landslide election victory in 1995 and kept his approval ratings between 70 and 80 percent until recently.
But the failure to impact poverty and reduce unemployment, or to raise wages, has cost Fujimori, with his popularity level below 50 percent.
Analysts said his handling of the hostage crisis was crucial to his political future.
"He's on a knife-edge. If this goes wrong, it will accentuate his fall in the polls. If it goes right, it will give him a much-needed surge of public support," said a Western diplomat.
"His power base is the Peruvian masses. With them he will go into the next century. Without them he's sunk."
